title: Turkey reports new fragment of world's oldest peace treaty at Hattusa
summary: The piece is said to preserve a 3,300-year-old clause that homes not be destroyed after fugitives were sent back — protection after forced return, not a right to remain — and the reading still awaits a published transcription and peer review.

claims.text: Scholarly caution: Articles 12-20 fugitive provisions are reciprocal extradition obligations between monarchs to return persons who fled, not modern refugee asylum or humanitarian protection. Arkeonews: 'These were diplomatic obligations negotiated between two ancient rulers, rather than asylum protections comparable to modern refugee law.'

sources.title: New Fragment of One of the World's Oldest Peace Treaties Found in Türkiye Reveals Ancient Rules for Fugitives

claims.text: What treaty actually requires vs ministerial gloss: broader fugitive clauses oblige each side to return fugitives and prohibit punishment/harm to returned individuals and families; the newly highlighted 'homes not be destroyed' wording sits inside that forced-return framework. This is a Bronze Age interstate control mechanism, not a right to remain or modern non-refoulement. Ersoy's framing as timeless protection of homes/human dignity inverts the clause's function (protection after forced return, not protection from return).

claims.text: Presentist media reproduction illustrates risk: SyriacPress headlined same fragment as 'provisions on the treatment of asylum seekers' and 'individuals seeking asylum,' while Arkeonews on same Ministry material cautions it is not asylum.

claims.text: Heritage-politics analysts note pattern of Türkiye instrumentalizing archaeology for soft power/nationalist narrative. Hyperallergic documents superlative claims ('firsts,' 'oldest,' 'center of civilization') to re-center Anatolia as epicenter of heritage, citing Lynn Meskell (UNESCO 'firsts/bests/onlys' incentivizing sensationalism), Bahar Aykan ('cultural heritage is not something that is just out there, free from human concerns'), and Kate Elizabeth Creasey (ethnonationalism drives battle for ancient heritage). Kadesh fragment's World Peace Day rollout fits this communications pattern.

sources.title: Discovery of 8,600-Year-Old Bread Gives Rise to Half-Baked Claims

claims.text: Heritage as political resource: The Art Newspaper documents new Turkish law allowing central government to seize historic properties from opposition-run municipalities, described as heritage becoming 'the latest front' and a 'Kulturkampf' where cultural assets provide income and legitimacy. Context supports analysts' caution that Hattusa/UNESCO announcements should be read also as state soft-power messaging, not purely scholarly communication.

sources.title: Turkey's heritage power grab: new law threatens Istanbul's opposition-run cultural sites

claims.text: No independent Egyptian, German Archaeological Institute, or international Hittitologist response to Ersoy's Palestine-linked framing or Articles 12-20 reading was located in sources reviewed. Absence of external corroboration leaves ministerial gloss as sole framing in circulation.
